solution: People are interchangeable and constrained only by per-room capacity, so a radius d works for a mentor in cell (r,c) exactly when A[r][c] >= 1 (the mentor must fit in his own room) and the total capacity of the (2d+1)x(2d+1) Chebyshev square centred on (r,c), clipped to the grid, is at least K+1; the answer is the smallest such d over all legal centres, and -1 when the whole grid holds fewer than K+1 people. That predicate is monotone in d because the square only grows, which licenses a binary search on d over [0, max(N,M)]. Each candidate d is tested by building a 2D prefix-sum table once and asking, for every cell with capacity at least 1, whether its clipped square sums to K+1 or more - an O(1) query per centre, so O(NM) per test. Total cost is O(NM log max(N,M)), about 2*10^7 operations for the worst allowed sum of N*M = 10^6, and O(NM) memory. The naive cell-by-cell square sum is far too slow (up to 10^6 centres times a square of up to 10^6 cells), and dropping the A[r][c] >= 1 check is wrong: on [[3,0,0,0,3]] with K=5 the illegal centre (0,2) would report 2 instead of the correct 4.
statement_summary: A school books a hotel whose rooms form an N by M grid, each with a stated capacity. One mentor and K students must be housed, and the task is the smallest Chebyshev distance from the mentor's room to the farthest room holding a student. The answer is -1 if total capacity is below K+1. The sum of N times M over all tests stays within one million.
notes: The curated 'Binary Search' topic hint holds up, but only as binary-search-answer: the answer d is searched over, and check(d) is a genuine O(NM) sweep of every legal mentor cell using 2D prefix-sum square queries, not a one-line monotonicity observation - so this is a real carrier rather than one of the 277 mislabelled ones. prefix-sum is listed as a first-class technique, not scaffolding: without O(1) square queries the check is up to 10^6 cells per centre and the intended complexity is unreachable; the vocabulary has no separate label for the 2D (inclusion-exclusion rectangle) form. Vocabulary gap: there is a manhattan-distance label but nothing for Chebyshev / chessboard distance, which is what max(|i1-i2|,|j1-j2|) is and is a query users would type for this problem; the L-infinity ball being an axis-aligned square is the whole reason prefix sums apply. Two subtleties a solver can miss - the mentor occupies one unit of his own room's capacity, so a zero-capacity cell cannot be a centre (verified by a dedicated test), and N and M are each up to 10^6 while N*M is bounded, so the grid can be an extremely thin strip and the binary-search range must be max(N,M), not something derived from N*M. Verification: all 4 samples, 4000 random grids and 600 thin 1xM/Nx1 grids against an all-(centre,d) brute force, 400 tiny grids against literal enumeration of every student distribution (confirming the capacity-sum reduction itself), and a monotonicity check of the predicate on 300 grids - all pass.
